S01About

Divisha Devaria

Lead, Business Development & Transformation, Ravi Infrabuild Projects Limited
Abu Dhabi, UAE

I work on the contractor side of Indian infrastructure, deciding which tenders are worth chasing and how to price them. For six years I've worked on bid strategy, estimation and market entry across highways, railways, airports and ropeways.

I completed an e-Masters in Data Science and Business Analytics at IIT Kanpur while working full time, and used it to build a bid decision tool in Python that reads a tender and tells the team whether the price needed to win is one they can live with. I'm now a Climatebase Fellow, working on how embodied carbon could enter Indian highway and railway tenders at the point where it can still be changed.

What ties it together

During my B.Tech I spent a week in the Netherlands studying how the Randstad plans for growth, water and mobility. I came home to work on roads designed around cars, while they were designing around people, bikes and water. That contrast is where my interest in how infrastructure decisions get made began. The courses, the IIT Kanpur degree, the bid tool and now the capstone all come back to it.

Research interests

Three questions I keep coming back to. Infrastructure procurement and financial risk: why cost and risk keep landing where they do on Indian projects, and what it would take to price carbon in at the tender stage. Data-driven decisions in capital-intensive settings: how to build tools that the people making real bid and investment calls will trust and use. Decarbonising the built environment through procurement: in a country that tenders new projects every day, the cheapest moment to cut embodied carbon is before the contract is signed.

Where I'm headed

Based in Abu Dhabi on a UAE residence visa, no sponsorship needed. Open to roles in infrastructure strategy, business development, data and climate-linked infrastructure, and to Master's and PhD programmes at the meeting point of infrastructure, data and decarbonisation.

S03Projects

Projects

What I built at work, the estimation behind it, and what I'm working on now.

BuiltPython and Streamlit · v7.2 · runs locally · used on 6 live tenders

Strategic Bid Intelligence Tool

Every tender a contractor looks at costs estimation time, and its bid security stays locked until the result is out. So choosing which tenders to chase is a business decision in itself. The tool answers one question before that money is spent: can we win this at a price we can live with?

It reads the tender PDF, predicts the range the winning bid is likely to land in against the authority's cost, and shows where RIPL's own estimate sits in that range. It then adds a weighted score for what a model can't see, such as competition, capacity and timing, and returns GO, CONDITIONAL GO or NO-GO with the reasoning written out.

one tender, assessed before the full estimation spend
01Tender PDF
02Parse
03Model
04Cost position
05Score
06Verdict
01 Tender PDFinput

The authority's notice inviting tender, RFP and technical schedules, uploaded as they are.

NIT · RFP · schedules
02 Parseextract

Pulls out the fields the model needs: sector, contract mode, authority, state, cost, length, construction type. Each one can be checked and corrected.

fields → editable form
03 Modelpredict

Recency-weighted Ridge regression on RIPL's bid history and market award data. Predicts the floor, mean and ceiling of the winning bid against authority cost, with the closest past tenders.

R² 0.641 · CV 0.438
04 Cost positioncompare

Places the internal estimate against that range and estimates the chance of winning at that price.

below floor · in range · above ceiling
05 Scorejudge

The bid team rates five things the data can't: competitive intensity, current capacity, strategic fit, governance and market timing. Each is weighted.

strategic score out of 100
06 Verdictoutput

Price position and strategic score combine into a verdict, with key factors and watch points. It informs the decision; the Technical Director makes it.

GO · CONDITIONAL GO · NO-GO
Segments Highway, Railway, Ropeway, AirportContract modes EPC, HAM, Item Rate

What it can't do

An R² of 0.641 and a cross-validated score of 0.438 mean the model narrows the range; it doesn't call the exact number. Segments with little data fall back on historical averages. The tool has been used on 6 live tenders but isn't formally deployed, and the final call stays with the Technical Director.

Where it came from

It grew out of the Excel Go/No-Go framework I designed in 2022 and my IIT Kanpur capstone, which tested the idea on 120 live bids and showed me, honestly, where it fell short.

Lifecycle cost model for a four-lane HAM highway

Under the hybrid annuity model the contractor maintains the road for the whole O&M period, so the bid has to price every year of upkeep, not just construction. This is the model I use to do it, built item by item from the bill of quantities.

01Inputslength, lanes, lane-km, plazas, O&M period
02Cost headsseven heads, each from quantities and rates
03Escalateevery head, year by year
04DiscountNPV and annualised NPV
05Expressas a share of bid project cost
SPV and professional feesMaintenance establishmentOperations: patrol, ambulance, crane, control roomRoutine maintenancePeriodic pavement renewalPower and lightingToll and traffic systems

What the cash flow looks like

Shape only, not to scale.

Steady yearly costs, then peaks when the pavement is renewed and when toll and traffic systems reach the end of their life. Renewals use hot recycling of the old pavement, and the toll plaza and roadside systems run on solar: the same thinking as my sustainable bid specifications.

In progressClimatebase Fellowship, Cohort 10 · Sep – Dec 2026 · Solo

Counting Carbon in Indian Transport Infrastructure Tenders

The problem. In Indian infrastructure, sustainability arrives after the decisions that fix a project's carbon footprint have already been made. Under lowest-bid award, contractors have no reason to measure carbon, and most have no means to either.

The proposal. A staged change led by the authority, which sets the baseline, not the contractor. It rewards before it requires, and gives contractors something to compete on besides lowest price.

Stage 1

Report

Contractors report embodied carbon from the existing bill of quantities, for a small bonus.

Stage 2

Reduce

A separate, larger bonus for real reduction, written into contract clauses.

Stage 3

Prequalify

Carbon performance becomes part of prequalification after 3 to 5 years.

bonuses build the data and the know-how
after 3 to 5 years
Today
0 of 13

tenders I reviewed asked for an embodied carbon figure.

Ideal state, 2030
Every new tender

from NHAI, MoRTH and the railways requires an embodied carbon figure worked out from the BoQ.

Scope: new NHAI, MoRTH and railway tenders. Projects already under way are out of reach; what can still change is what gets tendered next.

e-Masters, Data Science & Business Analytics

IIT Kanpur · completed 2024 · CPI 9.08 / 10 · studied while working full time

A few years into bids, I could see the biggest calls being made on instinct: which projects to chase, how to price risk, when to walk away. I chose IIT Kanpur for its grounding in statistics, and because I could study without stopping work.

Three projects from the degree, each with how the work flowed, what the data showed and the courses behind it. Grades for every course are at the end.

CapstoneMBA 944 · Grade A · supervised by Dr. Veena Bansal · solo

Predicting Competitive Bid Price for Infrastructure Projects

Can the winning bid on an Indian infrastructure tender be predicted, as a percentage of the authority's cost, before a contractor commits to a full estimate? I built the dataset myself from 120 live bids (2020–2023) across highway, railway and major structure projects.

Ridge did best. A cross-validation score of 0.44 then showed it didn't generalise yet.

The honest starting point

The model explained about two-thirds of the variance on test data, but the cross-validation score of 0.44 said it wouldn't hold up on new tenders. My conclusion was that bidders' risk appetite, and sometimes their urgency to win, drives much of the price, and that a bigger dataset was the way forward. That is where the Bid Intelligence Tool began: more data, recency weighting, and a decision layer on top.

A weekly rhythm

Lags where sales were strongly correlated with their own past.

Spikes every seventh day mean the week is the main cycle, so staffing and promotions should be planned day by day.

  • Promotion days consistently outsold other days.
  • Holiday months spiked, with December the highest.
  • Customer numbers drove sales more than anything else.

C

MBA 937 · Grade B+ · group of five · my part: the concept explanation, recommendations and extended model

Do Rural Roads Grow Local Economies?

A critical review of Asher and Novosad's study of PMGSY, India's national rural roads programme. The question is causal: do new roads make villages better off, or do villages that are already doing better simply get roads first? The study uses population cut-offs in the programme's own rules as a natural experiment.

How a fuzzy regression discontinuity works

Concept diagram, not data.

Villages just either side of the cut-off are alike in every other way, so the jump in road access works like a coin toss. It's "fuzzy" because crossing the cut-off raises the chance of a road without guaranteeing one.

What the roads changed

The paper's findings, as summarised in our review.

  • Transport serviceslarge, significant
  • Workers moving out of farmingsignificant
  • Jobs in village firmssmall (p = 0.09)
  • Farm yields and investmentvery small, not significant
  • Household assets and consumptionvery small, not significant

Roads improved access. On their own, they didn't make villages richer in the years the study covers.

Stage 1the threshold predicts who gets a road
Stage 2predicted access is linked to outcomes
Resulteffect for villages near the cut-off

Weighing the method

MethodStrength in this studyLimit in this study
Fuzzy RDDUses the population rule to approximate random assignment, and corrects for imperfect compliance.The estimate holds only near the cut-off and needs strong continuity assumptions.
Difference-in-differencesCompares trends before and after construction, beyond the cut-off.Relies on parallel trends, which may not hold across very different villages.
MatchingWorks when policy thresholds are unclear or not followed.Can't account for differences nobody measured.
Randomised trialThe gold standard: removes selection bias entirely.Impractical and hard to justify for building roads.

My extension: following the effect over time

The study measures outcomes four to six years after construction. To test longer-run effects without picking up other schemes by mistake, I proposed extending the second stage. Additions in amber.

Yv,d,t = β0 + β1Roadv,d,t + β2(popv,d − T) + β3(popv,d − T)·1{popv,d ≥ T} + β4Timet + β5(Roadv,d,t × Timet) + β6Policyv,d,t + ζXv,d + ηd,t + υv + εv,d,t

  • Road × Time shows whether the effect grows or fades over the years.
  • Policy controls for other schemes running in the same village.
  • ηd,t district-year fixed effects absorb regional change over time.
  • υv village fixed effects absorb what stays constant about each village.

Thesis

Final year · 2019Guide: Mr. Kannan Rayappan · Co-guide: Prof. Reshma Shah

PPP Construction Contracts: Financial Constraints and Mitigation

I studied six live BOT highway concessions through interviews with the people running them and a rebuild of each project's financials, then sorted their losses by cause. Land impediments accounted for 72% of the losses, far ahead of every other constraint.

The recommendations: land availability thresholds before bidding, realistic traffic studies, and mechanisms to hold schedules to account.

Building Inclusive Cities

How cities include and exclude people, and what planning can do about it. Two pieces of coursework below, both mine.

Coursework · Assignments 2 and 3 · hand-drawn

Ahmedabad: who the network reaches

First a mental map of the city: the wealthier corridor along the SG Highway in the west, the walled city and the river, and poorer settlements to the east and on the edges. Then the question that follows from it: does the transit network reach the people on the edge? My answer was a suggested BRTS connection linking a peripheral settlement in the south-west to the network.

Coursework · Assignments 4 and 5 · drawing redrawn from my map

Udaipur's walled city: from map to proposal

Udaipur is a mix with no clear borders between areas, except its old city. That walled core of about 2 sq km carries the city's identity, but streets no wider than 3.5 m are jammed with motor traffic. I mapped it, then wrote to the Chairman of the Urban Improvement Trust with a proposal, as the final assignment.

Peripheral roadCity wall PParking and cycle stands at the gatesInner streets for walking and cyclingWorst congestion
  1. Park motor vehicles in structures on the peripheral road, with safe bicycle stands beside them.
  2. Inside the walls, everything is within walking distance; cycle where walking isn't preferred.
  3. Give the inner streets to pedestrians and cyclists, in step with the city's ongoing conservation work.
"It is the people and place that make the sense of identifiable urban fabric."From my letter to the Urban Improvement Trust, December 2021
